entries.title: Morocco detains dozens of migrants trying to enter Spanish North African exclave Ceuta
entries.summary: The attempted crossings come two weeks after around 72,000 people rushed into the Spanish North African exclave from Morocco. Calls for another mass crossing had been circulating on social media this week.
entries.content:
August 16, 2026

The attempted crossings come two weeks after around 72,000 people rushed into the Spanish North African exclave from Morocco. Calls for another mass crossing had been circulating on social media this week.

Moroccan police on Saturday detained dozens of people who attempted to cross the border into the Spanish North African exclave of Ceuta.

It comes two weeks after around 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, which drove a wedge between Spain and other EU countries.

"This is a routine operation aimed at preventing attempted irregular migration" toward Ceuta, an official with knowledge of the intervention, who asked to remain anonymous, told AFP.

More than 100 migrants, mostly from sub-Saharan Africa, were stopped in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city across the border from Ceuta, a security source told Reuters.

Meanwhile, Morocco's Le360 media outlet reported that 294 people had been detained.

Calls on social media for mass crossings

Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring "the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin" calling for a mass crossing on August 15, and warned that both organizers and participants would face prosecution.

Eyewitnesses said there was a heavy Moroccan security presence around Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish exclave to the east.

Numerous checkpoints were set up, with patrol boats monitoring the coast and water cannons stationed at the border, according to Spain's public broadcaster RTVE.

Spanish media ordered to leave Fnideq

Spain's EFE news agency and RTVE said a representative from Morocco's Interior Ministry had ordered their journalists ​to leave Fnideq — known in Spanish as Castillejos — immediately without any explanation. The Moroccan official stated that he was "following instructions."

EFE president Miguel Angel Oliver urged Moroccan authorities to respect the free, "responsible and rigorous practice of journalism."

RTVE president Jose Pablo Lopez also demanded "full guarantees and the utmost respect" from Moroccan authorities so that his journalists could "freely practice their profession anywhere in the border region."

"The expulsion of our professionals from Castillejos represents a grave obstacle to press freedom and the right to information," Lopez said in a statement. 

Spain increases security after Ceuta border surge

Two weeks ago, around 72,000 people crossed into Ceuta over a few days, though most have since been returned to Morocco.

Some 100 people had died during the border surge.

Madrid has since beefed up security in the exclave, installing a maritime barrier and deploying more than 500 additional police from mainland Spain.

The Interior Ministry said they would remain in place as long as needed.

"We'll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality ‌as soon ​as possible and prevent events like those of July 30 from happening again," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Thursday.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Lebanon says 11 killed in Israeli airstrikes
entries.summary: Lebanon's prime minister denounced the attacks on villages in southern Lebanon for targeting civilians in their homes. Israel said it was firing on Hezbollah infrastructure.
entries.content:
Lebanon

Lebanon says 11 killed in Israeli airstrikes

August 15, 2026

Lebanon's prime minister denounced the attacks on villages in southern Lebanon for targeting civilians in their homes. Israel said it was firing on Hezbollah infrastructure.

At least 11 people were killed when Israel launched fresh airstrikes in southern Lebanon on Saturday, the deadliest since the Israel-Hezbollah truce nearly two months ago.

The attacks were met with defiance by the Iran-backed Hezbollah, which demanded an end to "humiliating" peace negotiations with Israel.

What do we know?

The Lebanese Health Ministry said one of the strikes, on the edge of the village of Ansar, killed seven people and wounded two.

The dead included three children and two women, according to the ministry.

The strike, which happened at dawn, hit a house and destroyed it, according to NNA, the Lebanese state news agency.

Germany's DPA news agency cited residents as saying the property served as a base for Hezbollah.

The second strike hit the village of Deir al-Zahrani, killing four and wounding 17.

NNA reported other strikes around the strategic Ali Taher hill, which overlooks parts of the southern city of Nabatiyeh and key roads to it.

The Israeli military confirmed hitting Hezbollah infrastructure in southern Lebanon, saying it was retaliation for an attack by the militia on Israeli forces.

Hezbollah vows revenge

Later Saturday, Hezbollah hit back at the latest strikes, saying they would be met with an "appropriate" response.

Israel "must clearly understand that its attacks, violations and attempts to impose a fait accompli cannot continue, and will be met with an appropriate response", the Iran-backed group said in a statement.

Hezbollah warned Lebanese authorities against continuing its "humiliating" negotiations with Israel, which would provide "the enemy with free concessions."

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam denounced the strikes, calling on Israel to "halt this escalation."

"The seven martyrs of the Israeli airstrike on the town of Ansar are not military infrastructure and the children and women killed were not military targets,” he wrote on X.

Ceasefire struggles to stick

The Israel–Hezbollah war reignited in early March around the start of the Iran war, when Hezbollah launched attacks on northern Israel to avenge the killing of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

It rapidly became a full-scale conflict that involved Israeli ground operations in southern Lebanon, mass evacuations of residents and the deaths of over 4,300 people.

Israel claims to have established the so-called security zone in southern Lebanon to prevent Hezbollah attacks on northern Israel.

According to Lebanese media, the Israeli-controlled area covers approximately 620 square kilometres, or about 6% of the country's total area.

Israel and Hezbollah have repeatedly accused each other of ceasefire violations following the announcement of a framework peace agreement in late June,

The deal lays out a plan for Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon, in return for Hezbollah laying down arms. It also envisions steps toward eventual peace.

The two sides have held seven rounds of talks; the most recent in Rome earlier this month.

Hezbollah refused direct talks, wasn't party to the deal and has refused to disarm.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Climate action doesn't seem to be a priority for Germany — despite heat-related deaths and drought. Why aren't more people taking to the streets?
entries.summary: Climate action does not seem to be a priority for the German government — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why aren't more people taking to the streets in protest?
entries.content:
August 15, 2026

Climate action does not seem to be a priority for the German government — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why aren't more people taking to the streets in protest?

When Lars Werner of the "Last Generation" climate activist group glued himself to the road four years ago to protest for greater climate action, Germany had not yet seen 12,500 heat-related deaths (the 2026 toll, so far), or record temperatures across Western Europe, and fully loaded ships were still navigating the Rhine without difficulty.

"Of course, I could say 'I told you so,' because it was foreseeable and comes as no surprise whatsoever," Werner told DW.

"The fact is, even back then, I was constantly explaining in my presentations that the Rhine would eventually run dry during hot summers and that this would have an incredible impact on the economy."

This summer, entire villages have been evacuated due to forest fires, farmers are expected to lose about 3 million metric tons of grain and rapeseed to drought, and hospital patients and the elderly in nursing homes are facing an acute threat to their lives in buildings with no air conditioning. 

But so far, the federal government has remained astonishingly quiet. Despite the crisis, it has still not convened a "heat summit."

"It is utterly irrational for the federal government to resort to tinkering with regulations — such as lifting the Sunday ban on truck traffic — in the hope of somehow scraping by without implementing a comprehensive climate protection policy for the long or even short term," said Werner.

Fridays for Future finds it difficult to motivate people

The government no longer has to worry about "Last Generation" protesters calling out its inaction by setting up road blockades. The climate activists halted their protests two years ago, worn down by hostility, fines and prison sentences. Now, the task of fiercely criticizing political decision-makers on climate policy falls primarily to the Fridays for Future Germany (FFF) movement.

"The federal government is doing virtually nothing when it comes to effective climate policy. Instead, various 'pseudo-solutions' are being promoted — such as dredging the Rhine to make it deeper or lifting the Sunday driving ban for trucks," FFF spokesperson Linda Kastrup told DW. She deplores what she sees as short-term fixes for the symptoms of the climate crisis, and notes that effectively nothing sustainable is being done.

Only a few hundred protesters turned out for a demonstration outside the chancellery in Berlin a week ago. It was a far cry from the protests in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to demand climate action.

A recent study by the Bertelsmann Foundation found that 80% of people in Germany are worried about climate change, and more than 50% want to see more government spending on climate protection. But that doesn't mean they're take to the streets.

Kastrup isn't surprised.

"When Chancellor Friedrich Merz completely dismisses and ignores climate policy — when we see tens of thousands of heat-related deaths in Germany alone yet not a single word is said about it — it inevitably leaves people with the impression in their private lives that climate protection doesn't matter. Naturally, that makes it very difficult to motivate people to take to the streets," she said.

In addition, there has been a rise in hateful speech directed at climate activists on social media.

"Two days ago, I posted a reel and within a very short time, there were 2,000 hateful comments on it," said Kastrup.

Focus has shifted to Ukraine, Gaza

Sebastian Haunss, a political science researcher at the University of Bremen, said it's surprising that the scorching summer of 2026 has not led to climate protests. He finds it remarkable that on the one hand, more and more people in Germany are installing solar power systems, but on the other, they take vacations on environmentally damaging cruise ships.

"A strong counter-position has emerged," he said. "Specifically, political actors like the AfD [the far-right populist Alternative for Germany Party — Editor's note] are pursuing an agenda that opposes climate protection regulations. Such actors — whether at the international or national level — did not exist just a few years ago."

Also, Haunss pointed out that large organizations like Fridays for Future have been replaced by a vast number of local groups, who operate largely out of the public eye. However, he believes a pivotal event could bring people back onto the streets in large numbers at any moment.

"Then there is the competition for attention; the COVID pandemic and the war in Ukraine pushed the climate issue out of the spotlight, and current economic concerns also play a major role," said Haunss, adding that many of those who took to the streets against climate change a few years ago are now focusing on different topics.

"In some cases, their issues have shifted, and other topics — such as the war in Gaza and solidarity with Palestine — have moved to the forefront."

A divided government

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) now wants to amend the constitution, the Basic Law, to make heat protection a joint responsibility of the federal government, the states, and the municipalities.

However, the larger coalition partner, the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), is skeptical of the plan and has cited "legal concerns."

"Within the coalition, I do indeed see us — the SPD — as the bulwark for energy transition to renewables," Nina Scheer, energy policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group, told DW. "All my colleagues in our parliamentary group would like to achieve more in terms of climate protection. But we also have to accept setbacks regarding climate measures in order to maintain unity within the coalition."

For instance, Scheer said, she voted in favor of making air travel cheaper and expanding regional airports, although she personally finds it wrong.

Scheer has long advocated for a faster expansion of renewable energy, and does not see eye to eye with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU), who favors gas over wind and solar power for energy supply.

"Reiche goes around pushing the narrative that while we do want climate protection and remain committed to the goals, renewables are simply too expensive. And to that, one has to say: 'No, that is simply not true,'" said Scheer.

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement and the national Climate Action Act, Germany has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2045. However, recent statements by some politicians have raised doubts as to whether the federal government is pursuing this goal with great determination.

"We cannot halt climate change from Germany alone," Chancellor Friedrich Merz said recently, a statement that Scheer considered disastrous.

"Fundamentally, it is a rejection of greater climate action, even though we ought to be stepping up our efforts," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Hawaii under state of emergency ahead of historic hurricane
entries.summary: A hurricane is forecast to hit the Big Island of Hawaii this weekend, bringing heavy rain and wind. Should it make landfall, Lala would be the first hurricane to hit the island since 1871.
entries.content:
August 15, 2026

A hurricane is forecast to hit the Big Island of Hawaii this weekend, bringing heavy rain and wind. Should it make landfall, Lala would be the first hurricane to hit the island since 1871.

Residents on the Big Island of Hawaii, which gives its name to the volcanic US Pacific archipelago, are preparing for a potentially historic weather situation with a tropical storm gathering hurricane-level strength as it approaches.

The US Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) National Hurricane Center (NHC) on Friday said Lala, a powerful tropical storm at the moment, should be at hurricane strength by the time it approaches the Big Island on Saturday.

Hawaii Governor Josh Green, who called the storm "enormous," declared a state of emergency on Friday in an effort to make sure the state and its counties "have sufficient resources to clear debris, secure infrastructure and take other measures to prepare."

Currently, a hurricane warning is in effect for Hawaii County, which covers the Big Island. The islands of Maui, Molokai and Kahoolawe to its northwest are under a tropical storm warning.

Should the storm make landfall as expected, it would be the first time the Big Island has been hit by a hurricane since 1871.

The storm is expected to bring winds, rainfall and heavy surf, spurring government and residents to prepare for the worst.

Shelters have already been set up and residents encouraged to remain vigilant and get themselves and their families to safe spaces before they become trapped.

What if Lala doesn't make landfall?

Experts say a direct hit is not necessarily the concern here, with meteorologist Vanessa Almanza of the National Weather Service (NWS) in Honolulu cited by the Associated Press as saying: "It doesn't take landfall to create destruction. A lot of the impacts are felt outside of the hurricane."

The National Hurricane Center predicts 8 to 12 inches (20.3 to 30.5 centimeters) of rain across Maui and the Big Island this weekend, with maximum totals as high as 25 inches (63.5 centimeters) in some Big Island locations.

The NHC also warned that the storm could bring "life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," as well as dangerous storm surges and ocean swells, "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."

Conditions trigger fear of floods and fires

As of Friday afternoon, Lala was located about 275 miles (440 kilometers) east-southeast of South Point, Hawaii, according to the NHC.

Data showed the storm had maximum sustained winds of 65 miles per hour (100 kilometers per hour) and was moving toward the west-northwest at 14 miles per hour. The wind-speed threshold for a Category 1 hurricane is 74 miles per hour.

Beyond fear of flooding, which the island of Oahu experienced in March, dry and windy weather has increased fear of wildfires as the storm picks up pace.

In 2023, the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds caused by a hurricane passing by far to the south.

Pointing to 1992's Hurricane Iniki as a tale of warning

The last hurricane to make landfall on the archipelago was Iniki, a category 4 storm, in 1992 — also an El Nino year.

On Friday, Governor Green reminded residents that Iniki made landfall after changing its path, "so we just can never know if a storm is going to turn."

While urging vigilance, Green said: "It did $3 billion (€2.6 billion) in damage. It destroyed thousands of homes and it did kill six people."

Green implored residents: "If you feel now that your house doesn't have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first you go to a family or friend's house and you kind of hunker down there."

The southern end of Hawaii is remote and rural but its affordability has attracted a growing population, some of whom live off-grid in unpermitted structures.

'Prepare, don't wait' say authorities

On neighboring Oahu, Honolulu Mayor Rick Blangiardi said Friday: "I am asking everyone to finish your preparations today. Don't wait for the weather to deteriorate. Stay informed, stay away from dangerous areas and make sure your family knows what to do if conditions worsen."

Residents were encouraged to clean gutters and drains, clear any hanging branches or debris from yards and seal their doors, with emergency services adding, "Stay away from beaches and coastal areas where rough surf and rip currents could sweep you away."

This year's Pacific Ocean El Nino has already attained temperatures so high that when it peaks between October and December NOAA says there is a 69% chance of a "historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Nino events dating back to 1950."

The natural climate pattern occurs when ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific become unusually warm. This tends to fuel hurricane activity in the Pacific while retarding it in the Atlantic.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Russians snap up new homes built on Ukraine 'graveyard'
entries.summary: Russia is constructing high-rises in the occupied Ukrainian city of Mariupol, on the sites of buildings it destroyed. Who's buying these properties? And what happened to the Ukrainians who used to lived here?
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russians snap up new homes built on Ukraine 'graveyard'

August 15, 2026

Russia is constructing high-rises in the occupied Ukrainian city of Mariupol, on the sites of buildings it destroyed. Who's buying these properties? And what happened to the Ukrainians who used to lived here?

Halyna Artemova, an English teacher, lived in Mariupol for almost 40 years, at Metallurgy Avenue 87.

"It's my beloved city. When I look at the photos, it brings tears to my eyes. I know every crack in the asphalt, every tree," she told DW. Her apartment block in the city on the Sea of Azov was struck by a missile during a Russian attack in March 2022.

Photographer Yevhen Sosnovsky and his wife lived in the house next door, Metallurgy Avenue 85, for 20 years. "I did everything myself, all the interior renovations, and the furniture," he said. "We invested a lot in it; we planned to spend our twilight years there, living quietly." His building also caught fire during the missile attack, and residents were driven out by Russian troops. They weren't even allowed to take food or clothing with them.

Now there's a parking lot where Sosnovsky's apartment block used to be. Next door, where Artemova once lived, stands a new building. The Russian building contractor Su-2007, which operates in the Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, cleared several buildings on Metallurgy Avenue that were destroyed in the war and constructed high-rise apartment blocks in their place. These form part of a residential complex now known as the Leningradsky Kvartal.

"They're building on human bones, and fast, to eradicate the traces of their crimes," said Sosnovsky.

DW is not allowed in to the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, so cannot report directly from city. However, it is possible to get an idea of what life is like in Mariupol today by talking to people who used to live there, studying satellite images, and doing research online.

Newcomers benefit from cheap mortgages

Many people who have moved into the new apartments on Metallurgy Avenue communicate with each other online in neighborhood forums. From these forums, it's clear that the majority bought the apartments either to live in themselves, or to rent out.

In chats, they ask how they can get furniture delivered from Russia, or which kindergarten or school they should choose for their children. People are reminded that the most important thing when submitting documents is that they should be of Russian origin.

Not everyone has finished remodeling their apartments, and some people with small children take the opportunity to complain: "It's too late! Stop the goddamn renovations! Or maybe you're pro-Ukrainian and oppose Russian laws?"

Economist Vyacheslav Shiryaev said apartments in the new buildings in Mariupol are being bought primarily by incomers: Russian security personnel, officials and people working in military logistics. "In addition, there are some who would just like to live by the sea but can't afford Crimea or Sochi," he said.

In the Russian-occupied regions, people are offered cheap mortgages at an annual interest rate of 2% for the whole period of the mortgage — provided the borrower has Russian citizenship. The maximum they can borrow is 6 million rubles (around €63,000/$72,000), and they must be able to put down a deposit of at least 2%.

Property prices have soared

Dozens of apartment blocks are being built in Mariupol, and many are already occupied. Russian banks report that the port city in the occupied region tops the list for mortgage loans. Property prices have risen by a third in just one year, primarily because of the coastal location.

You won't find a location like this in Russia, said Shiryaev. However, he pointed out that the apartments are of very bad quality. "Construction companies are cutting corners wherever they can, but still demanding exorbitant prices," he said.

The Leningradsky Kvartal residential complex, 15 buildings of 12 to 15 floors each, is near the center of town and just 10 minutes' drive from the sea. One- and two-room apartments cost between 7.5 million and almost 10 million rubles (€104,000). Three-room apartments can be bought for upwards of 10 million rubles. Newcomers to the region are offered discounts of up to 12%.

In the chats, people living in the complex say they have insured their mortgages "against war risks." If their building is destroyed, they won't have to pay back their loan. They will, however, lose their apartment.

Nobody in the forum talks about the fact that there were other people living on the site of Leningradsky Kvartal just a few years ago.

Dead and wounded in Mariupol

According to the United Nations, 90% of the buildings in Mariupol were damaged or destroyed in the 2022 siege. Media outlets estimate that tens of thousands of people were killed. Former residents of Metallurgy Avenue told DW of neighbors who were killed or injured.

"A man and his son from the building next door were killed when they went out to fetch water," said Artemova. "In house number 89, a woman was buried beneath a concrete slab after a missile strike and died. A missile struck the first floor of house number 91, and a family was killed."

Artemova herself was wounded by shrapnel, but managed to leave Mariupol with her elderly mother and her son. Sosnovsky was hit by a bullet. He too fled the city, with his wife and mother-in-law.

Many of those who lived in buildings that were hit, but whose apartments were not destroyed, have remained in the city. However, DW was told that the occupying authorities demanded they leave their apartments nonetheless. They were promised new apartments in exchange.

But a source told DW that none of the inhabitants of the former blocks on Metallurgy Avenue was allocated an apartment in the new Leningradsky Kvartal buildings. And those who had lost everything in the attacks could not afford a mortgage. Another source told DW that people were put in accommodation on the outskirts of town, or else in hostels.

'We were robbed of our good life'

The majority of those who fled do understand why their former neighbors stayed in the city. Not everyone had the possibility of leaving Mariupol and starting again elsewhere.

"The local population is being pushed out of Mariupol," said Artemova, who now lives in Kyiv with her son. Like others DW spoke with who had left the city, she said Mariupol had started to develop rapidly a few years before the Russian invasion in early 2022. People wanted to live there.

"We were robbed of our ordinary life, which may have been uninteresting for some, but it was a good life. We'd go to market, knew where to buy what; we'd have a coffee, bump into a school friend with her dog and say hello," she remembered.

Neither Artemova nor Sosnovsky are considering returning to their hometown and re-registering their apartments according to the regulations of the Russian occupying authority. It's not even clear whether or not they would be allowed to enter the zone. But Ukraine is not compensating people for the loss of property there, as its authorities can't assess the situation without access to the occupied region.

"They're building their shiny new houses on what used to be a graveyard. I'd like nothing better than to bomb them, but only when no one's in the buildings. It's enough to drive you to despair," said one former resident of Metallurgy Avenue. He too lived there for decades, and remembers his child's first steps, taken in an apartment that no longer exists.

This is how he describes the city today: "In the center it's still OK, but if you go just a little to the left or right it smells of death."

This article was originally written in Russian.

entries.title: Afghan allies still waiting for the safety Germany promised
entries.summary: After the Taliban retook power on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring Afghan staff to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
entries.content:
Germany

Afghan allies still waiting for the safety Germany promised

August 15, 2026

After the Taliban retook power on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring Afghan staff to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

It's hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June 2026, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.

Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."

In August 2026, five years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany.

He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable," he said.

New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union and the center-left Social Democrats under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government has remained firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2,500 ($,2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.

Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission program for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry has maintained it is in the right. "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."

According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.

German aid organization continues support

Javad Niazi and his family continue to worry for their future. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport in August 2021, the German nongovernmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning. "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people," she told DW. "And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be four weeks has now become five years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans — with success. They've won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," said Beyer.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was canceled," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

Correction, August 15, 2026: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that Alexander Dobrindt is Germany's foreign minister. He is the German interior minister. DW apologizes for the mistake.

entries.title: Trump's Latin America allies open arms to Israel
entries.summary: While ongoing military actions in Gaza and settler attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have largely isolated Israel globally, Latin America's authoritarian right sees an opening for a strategic alliance.
entries.content:
Latin America

Trump's Latin America allies open arms to Israel

August 15, 2026

While ongoing military actions in Gaza and settler attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have largely isolated Israel globally, Latin America's authoritarian right sees an opening for a strategic alliance.

A three-week military offensive in the Gaza Strip in 2009, which killed more than 1,400 people, including an estimated 1,100 civilians, spurred Venezuela's Socialist president at the time, Hugo Chavez, to expel the Israeli ambassador in protest and end diplomatic relations.

Seventeen years later, Venezuela and Israel have agreed to establish a mechanism for the resumption of consular services. It's a limited step, but one that until recently would have been unthinkable.

In Colombia, the nationalist government of new President Abelardo de la Espriella recently reversed the decision by his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, to sever diplomatic relations with Israel in protest of the country's most recent war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 people, nearly one-third of them children.

De la Espriella has even announced that Colombia will relocate its embassy to Jerusalem, and this week declared that Colombia would join the United States as the only two countries that recognize "Israeli sovereignty" over the Golan Heights, which is Syrian territory under international law but has been occupied by Israel since 1967. The vast majority of the international community, including Germany and the UN, does not recognize the annexation of the Golan Heights by Israel.

"There is a trend toward rapprochement with Israel as a response to the surge of the radical right in the region," said Isaac Caro, a professor at Alberto Hurtado University in Chile. Caro said authoritarians in Latin America were linking relations with Israel to "an active alignment with US foreign policy." He said reinforcing ties with Israel had become a characteristic of Latin America's radical right as part of the renewed discourse of region's place in Judeo-Christian Western civilization.

In Argentina, for example, ultraconservative President Javier Milei has made close relations with Israel a defining feature of both his foreign policy and his own political identity.

Daniel Wajner, associate professor of international relations at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said there had been a "surge" in diplomacy between Israel and Latin American governments. Wajner said Jair Bolsonaro, the neoliberal former president of Brazil, and El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the self-described "world's coolest dictator," were early adopters of warmer ties with Israel. They were followed by Milei and others.

Wajner said Latin America's authoritarians were actively "embracing" the national-conservative government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He also said there were ideological, religious and strategic factors in governments' tightening of bonds with the country, such as the desire to signal a like-minded international orientation with the US.

Gilberto Aranda, a political analyst from the University of Chile, said there had been a trend in Latin America of authoritarians' aligning with the US under Donald Trump — and therefore also engaging in rapprochement with Israel.

Colombia's new president triggers 'fundamental shift'

In 2024, under Petro, Colombia broke off relations because of the war in Gaza. In the week since de la Espriella assumed office on August 7, Caro said there has been a "fundamental shift" in Colombia's foreign policy.

In Venezuela, the stated policies of the current government, which took power after US forces abducted the sitting president in early January, remain rooted in the socialist populism of Chavismo. However, the resumption of consular services has proved a symbolic diplomatic success for Israel.

Bolivia's Socialist government severed relations with Israel after the bombardment of a camp for displaced people in Gaza in 2023. When the conservative Rodrigo Paz assumed office 2025, he quickly restored ties.

In Chile, the democratic socialist former president, Gabriel Boric, was highly critical of Netanyahu and his government. His successor, the national conservative, Jose Antonio Kast, is seeking, among other things, to revive Chile's defense cooperation with Israel.

Brazil, Mexico maintain 'critical stance' toward Israel

By contrast, the social-democratic government of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil has taken a highly critical stance toward Israeli actions in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.

"The country with the most influence in the region, which maintains a critical stance toward Israel, is clearly Brazil," said Aranda. Brazil's demographic, economic and political clout are a major counterweight to the shift by other Latin American governments toward warmer relations with Israel.

Then there is Mexico, the other giant of Latin America. Whereas Lula, in Brazil, is particularly critical, Mexico, under President Claudia Sheinbaum, is trying to preserve greater neutrality as well as a diplomatic balance. Sheinbaum has criticized Israel's actions in Gaza, but still maintains diplomatic relations. This shows that criticism of the Netanyahu government does not inevitably signify the breakdown of relations with the state of Israel.

Still, given the recent mass killings in Gaza, the shift in Israel's relations with some governments in Latin America is significant. Israel is not just interested in winning over friendly governments. These bilateral relationships date back to the foundation of the Israeli state in 1948, and cover migration, trade, and security. The support of Latin America in multilateral organizations such as the United Nations has always been key in countering Israel's international isolation.

Wajner said the decision by Latin American governments to improve ties with Israel offered both sides "legitimacy, cooperation and influence." Israel needs international partners, and Latin American goverments also offer opportunities for economic, technological and military cooperation. For its part, Latin America can turn to Israel as a strong partner in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and defense.

Though Israel has managed to forge new bonds in Latin America for now, long-term relations will continue to depend on who is in power, where and when.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: India: Modi promises free exam coaching, AI training for youth after protests
entries.summary: Speaking on India's Independence Day, PM Modi announced free online coaching for competitive exams and AI training for 10 million youths, weeks after protests over alleged exam paper leaks and recruitment irregularities.
entries.content:
India

India: Modi promises exam coaching, AI training for youth

August 15, 2026

Speaking on India's Independence Day, PM Modi announced free online coaching for competitive exams and AI training for 10 million youths, weeks after protests over alleged exam paper leaks and recruitment irregularities.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on India's Independence Day announced training in artificial intelligence (AI) skills as well as free online coaching for young people for competitive exams just weeks after youth-led protests over exam paper leaks and recruitment irregularities.

Speaking at the Red Fort in New Delhi on Saturday, Modi said the coaching initiative would help ease the financial burden on poor and middle-class families.

"The competition surrounding coaching classes has become a huge burden for middle-class families," Modi said, adding that students could stay with their families while preparing for exams.

Modi's promise comes as last month the country was rocked by protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over alleged irregularities in competitive exams.

The protests ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan highlighting widespread concerns over access to education and jobs.

10 million youths to train in AI skills

The Indian prime minister also said 10 million young people would receive training in AI skills over the next year, in a move to appease the nation's youth that forced the Modi government to face its biggest challenge since coming to power in 2014.

Modi also said India will have eight more semiconductor chip plants in the coming years and five nuclear reactors which will generate 100 gigawatts of power by 2047.

In a speech lasting more than an hour, Modi outlined a seven-point growth and reform framework aimed at making India a developed country within 20 years. The plan focuses on manufacturing, agriculture, technology, defense and sectors including tourism and handicrafts.

Modi warns against 'intellectual Naxals'

At the same time, Modi also took aim at the latest enemy of the state — the "intellectual Naxals."

This was a reference to India's Naxal movement, which waged a guerrilla-style insurgency against the government, particularly in central and eastern India, leaving thousands dead and injured over nearly 60 years.

Modi said his government had defeated the armed movement but warned that the fight against the "Naxal mentality" remained, as its adherents looked for "opportunities to create violence and unrest."

Modi said these "intellectual Naxals" had to be identified and isolated to connect young people with the mainstream. Modi did not specify who these "intellectual Naxals" were in his speech.

In the past, Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has labelled rights activists, academics and intellectuals, journalists, political opponents, government critics and others with left-wing views as "urban Naxals."

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Germany: Berlin techno fans pause for Pride attack victims
entries.summary: Rave the Planet is taking place under high security after last month's deadly Islamist attack. Also: Russia labels another German institute as "undesirable." DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Berlin techno fans pause for Pride attack victims

Published August 15, 2026last updated August 15, 2026

Rave the Planet is taking place under high security after last month's deadly Islamist attack. Also: Russia labels another German institute as "undesirable." DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog has closed. Below is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on August 15, 2026:

  • Russia adds Germany's Research Centre for East European Studies (FSO) to its list of 'undesirable' organizations
  • A techno parade in Berlin takes place under heightened security following last month's deadly attack during a Pride march
  • Johannes Liebmann breaks the world record in the men's 1,500m freestyle at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

For coverage of the wildfire in western Germany, head over to our dedicated blog here.

Skip next section Germany's Weber clinches another European javelin gold

Germany's Weber clinches another European javelin gold

Germany's Julian Weber has won European Championship gold in the javelin throw for the second time.

The 31-year-old overcame shoulder issues to finish ahead of his teammate Nick Thumm with his final throw of 90.40 meters.

"I just wanted to show that I'm a mental beast. I’m so glad it worked out. I’m incredibly happy," Weber told ZDF public television.

Four years ago, he also secured a javelin gold at the European Championships in Munich.

Germany now sits third in the medal table with four golds, behind Italy and the United Kingdom.

On Friday, German sprinter Owen Ansah won the 200-meter final despite facing a potential ban from the National Anti-Doping Agency of Germany for allegedly failing to comply with a doping test.

Skip next section Germany's Johannes Liebmann breaks world record in men's 1,500m freestyle

Germany's Johannes Liebmann breaks world record in men's 1,500m freestyle

German teenager Johannes Liebmann set a new world record in the men's 1,500 meter freestyle with a time of 14 minutes, 26.79 seconds at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris.

Liebmann, who is 19 years old, beat the previous record of 14 minutes, 30.67 seconds, that had been held by American Bobby Finke since the 2024 Olympics.

Liebmann set out a cracking pace from the very beginning, with spectators cheering him on to the finish line over the final 200 meters.

Hungary's Zalan Sarkany won the silver medal, and Liebmann's teammate Oliver Klemet won the bronze medal.

Liebmann, who was taking part in his first European Championships, won the 800-meter freestyle earlier this week too.

Skip next section President calls for end to fear after Berlin Pride attack

President calls for end to fear after Berlin Pride attack

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has urged society to protect the LGBTQ+ community against attacks like the van ramming and stabbing near the Berlin Pride parade three weeks ago.

On July 25, an Islamist attacker drove a van into a crowd and then allegedly attacked people with a machete, killing a woman and injuring at least 31 people.

"In an open society, everyone must be able to follow their own path," Steinmeier wrote in an article for the Zeit Online website.

This right applies "not only without fear, but also with pride; not only in private, but also in public," he asserted.

"Everyone has the right to self-determination, particularly where it concerns the very core of every human being — the expression of one's own personality, love and partnership, physicality and sexuality," the head of state continued.

Steinmeier said the attack primarily targeted queer people, leaving many afraid.

He stressed that a robust democracy cannot tolerate this and must prioritize law enforcement, public safety and education.

The head of state made the comments as several smaller German cities held their own Pride events this weekend, including Darmstadt, Bayreuth, Krefeld and Münster.

Skip next section Berlin's Rave the Planet techno event starts with moment of silence

Berlin's Rave the Planet techno event starts with moment of silence

As tens of thousands of partiers gathered for "Rave the Planet" — a Berlin music event labeling itself a political demonstration — there was quiet before organizers began blasting music.

The now high-security event began with a moment of silence for the victims of an Islamist attack on an LGBTQ+ pride event at the same spot three weeks ago. 

Taking place under the motto "imagine love," Rave the Planet is the first major party event in the German capital since the July 25 terror attack.

A Christopher Street Day (CSD) organizer invited to Saturday's event called on those gathered to "be courageous" … "especially now."

A large police presence is on hand to protect revelers, streets and paths have been closed and trams will not stop at regular destinations as a result of the event.

Skip next section Rhine water levels fall again

Rhine water levels fall again

Water levels on the Rhine River have fallen to new record lows, greatly disrupting river-borne cargo transport, as a prolonged dry spell continues in most of Germany.

According to the inland navigation agency WSV, the water level gauge at the Kaub bottleneck near Koblenz fell to 6 centimeters (2.4 inches) late on Friday and was 8 cm ​early on Saturday.

Until this year, the previous lowest level marked by the gauge was 25 cm recorded ‌in 2018.

The gauge gives the depth over an arbitrary baseline near the bank of the river, but is an indication of the navigable depth at that point, which is around a meter (3 feet) deeper.

Most cargo previously transported on the Rhine has been shifted to road and rail, but these transport methods cannot fully compensate for the heavy loads carried by ships.

For this reason, companies have ​started to report disruption to their supplies, with chemical producers, utilities, steelmakers warning of higher costs, transport bottlenecks and reduced production.

Skip next section Bonn authorities warn of potential danger after ordnance find

Bonn authorities warn of potential danger after ordnance find

Authorities in the western city of Bonn have called on people to avoid an area of the Rhine riverbank in the Gronau district after ordnance was found there.

They said they would provide more information on any evacuation measures and street closures as it became available.

The ordnance was found not far from DW's Bonn headquarters, meaning that any evacuation order could also affect the international broadcaster.

The danger level has so far been described as "slight."

Skip next section Potentially toxic algae spread in Germany's north

Potentially toxic algae spread in Germany's north

Health authorities have issued warnings to bathers as potentially toxic blue-green algae thrive in waters in the north of Germany.

When high concentrations occur in water, the algae can cause allergic reactions and irritation to skin and mucous membranes, and nausea and vomiting if ingested in sufficient quantities.

Satellite images from the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency show large patches of the algae — which are, in fact, cyanobacteria — in the Baltic Sea off the coast between Rostock and Hiddensee island, extending across the sea to the Danish coast.

They have also been found in lakes in the state of Schleswig-Holstein. Swimming in them has been banned until, probably, Wednesday.

The government in the state of Mecklenburg-Vorpomerania has warned against swimming in the sea when bathers can no longer see their feet in knee-high water.

Skip next section AfD politician allegedly attacks 14-year-old — reports

AfD politician allegedly attacks 14-year-old — reports

A politician from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is being investigated over an alleged attack on a 14-year-old boy found defacing one of the party's campaign posters, the Spiegel newsmagazine and other media have reported.

The incident in the city of Stendal occurred just weeks before an election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

The Spiegel cited the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) as saying that the boy, along with other youths, was caught in the act of damaging an AfD poster.

"Subsequently, there was a possible physical altercation between a person with immunity and the youths. In the course of this, a blunt instrument was allegedly used," the LKA is quoted as saying.

It said one of the youths was slightly injured and received medical treatment.

Spiegel cited sources close to the boy as saying he suffered slight concussion, several bruises and injuries to his lip.

The public-service broadcaster MDR said the "blunt instrument" concerned was a baseball bat.

Skip next section Heightened security planned at Berlin techno parade

Heightened security planned at Berlin techno parade

The techno parade Rave the Planet is expected to draw tens of thousands of people in Berlin in Saturday, with police stepping up security at the event after last month's Islamist attack on fringes of the Pride march in the capital.

Participants in the parade will also have to contend with high temperatures of up to 37 C (98.6 F).

Police say they will deploy at least one water cannon to spray a cooling water mist and free drinking water is to be made available along the route of the parade, organizers have said.

The parade is to start in the early afternoon and run until late in the evening.

It is planned to run along the main boulevard through the Tiergarten park, between the Brandenburg Gate and the Victory Column, close to the site of the July 25 attack, in which an Islamist assailant killed a woman and injured at least 31 people, some seriously.

A police spokeswoman said some 1,500 officers would be deployed at the event, with Berlin police supported by colleagues from the states of Brandenburg and Saxony-Anhalt.

The techno parade was first held in Berlin in 2022 to celebrate electronic music culture and has taken place every year since then.

Organizers have registered 300,000 participants, though police have put the number closer to 100,000 at previous parades.

Skip next section Russia lists another German research body as 'undesirable'

Russia lists another German research body as 'undesirable'

On Friday, Russia's Justice Ministry added the Research Centre for East European Studies (FSO), based at the University of Bremen, to its list of "undesirable" organizations

Such organizations are banned from carrying out activities within Russia's territory.

The public prosecutor's office claims that the FSO aims to lobby the US government to impose sanctions on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine.  

According to the research institute's website, it is "a place where the Eastern Bloc and its societies, with their specific cultures, are studied, and where current developments in the post-Soviet region are analyzed."

Russia's list of "undesirable" organizations already contains several German ones, including Deutsche Welle (DW), the German Historical Institute (DHI), which has been active in Moscow for many years, the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and numerous political foundations.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the — ever-drier — Rhine River in Bonn.

The most important story in Germany at present is, of course, the wildfire raging in the western Eifel region. We have a dedicated blog on the catastrophe that you can find here.

In our Germany news blog, we will thus be covering a range of other stories.

Russia has listed yet another German organization as "undesirable" as it continues to clamp down on free speech.

They include a techno parade in the capital, Berlin, which is to take place under heightened security after last month's deadly attack during a Pride march at a nearby location.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is also in the news as one of its members is investigated after allegedly injuring a 14-year-old caught defacing a campaign poster.

Read on here for more on the latest from Germany.

entries.title: US: FDA recalls 19 million eggs over salmonella risk
entries.summary: The US has issued a serious health warning over the recalled eggs, saying exposure to the potentially contaminated products could cause severe illness or death.
entries.content:
August 15, 2026

The US has issued a serious health warning over the recalled eggs, saying exposure to the potentially contaminated products could cause severe illness or death.

Around 19 million eggs have been recalled in the United States over possible salmonella contamination, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has said.

Midwest Poultry Services (MPS) voluntarily recalled 1,589,577 dozen eggs on July 22 after detecting potential Salmonella Enteritidis contamination at two Texas farms, the FDA said.

MPS Egg Farms said on its website that it had proactively recalled the eggs as a precautionary measure and initiated testing protocols to identify potential sources of salmonella.

On Wednesday, the FDA said it was a Class 1 recall, indicating a reasonable probability of serious illness or death.

What did the FDA say about the egg recall?

The eggs were produced between June 6 and July 3 and distributed in the states of Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico and Mississippi.

These included both white shell eggs and brown cage-free shell eggs.

They were sold under several brand names, with sell-by or best-by dates from July 20 to August 17.

According to the FDA advisory:

  • Consumers should throw away the recalled eggs or return them for a refund
  • Restaurants and retailers should not serve or sell the eggs
  • Consumers, restaurants, and retailers who purchased or received recalled eggs should carefully clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers that the recalled eggs touched.
